quiz.q: A patient found hypotensive overnight has an AST of 3,400 U/L and an ALT of 2,900 U/L with a markedly elevated LDH. By the next morning both have fallen by half. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.why: A massive transaminase spike with a very high LDH immediately after hypotension, followed by a rapid fall once perfusion returns, is shock liver. Viral hepatitis falls over weeks, alcoholic hepatitis keeps enzymes under about 300 U/L, and obstruction is a cholestatic pattern.

quiz.q: An acetaminophen overdose patient has ALT 7,200 U/L, bilirubin 1.6 mg/dL, INR 4.1, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.24, and grade 3 encephalopathy. Which values determine prognosis?
choices: The bilirubin, since it is nearly normal
The INR, creatinine, pH, and encephalopathy grade
The ALT, since it is highest
quiz.why: Transaminase height measures cells already destroyed. Survival depends on whether the remaining liver can support the patient, which is captured by coagulopathy, renal failure, acidosis, and encephalopathy — the elements of transplant criteria.

quiz.q: A 15-year-old athlete has an alkaline phosphatase of 410 U/L with a normal GGT, normal bilirubin, and normal transaminases. What does this indicate?
choices: Bone origin, normal for a growing adolescent
quiz.why: Alkaline phosphatase exists in both liver and bone isoforms. A normal GGT excludes a hepatobiliary source, and growing bone produces large amounts in adolescence. Obstruction would raise GGT and direct bilirubin.

quiz.q: A cirrhotic patient with abdominal pain has ascitic fluid with 410 neutrophils per microliter and a serum-to-ascites albumin gradient of 1.6 g/dL. The culture is pending. What should be done?
choices: No treatment; the albumin gradient explains the fluid
Start antibiotics now for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
quiz.why: A neutrophil count of 250 per microliter or more defines spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and is treated immediately, since cultures are negative in a substantial minority of true cases. The albumin gradient identifies portal hypertension as the cause of ascites, not infection.

quiz.q: A patient with recurrent deep vein thromboses has an aPTT of 58 seconds that fails to correct on a 1:1 mix with normal plasma. What does this indicate?
choices: An inhibitor, most likely a lupus anticoagulant
quiz.why: Correction on mixing means a factor was missing and was supplied; failure to correct means something in the plasma is inhibiting the reaction. In a patient who clots rather than bleeds, that inhibitor is a lupus anticoagulant, which prolongs the test in vitro while causing thrombosis in vivo.

quiz.q: A patient on apixaban has a head injury. The PT is 13.1 and the aPTT is 30 seconds, both normal. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The patient must have been taking warfarin instead
The drug has cleared and reversal is unnecessary
Normal conventional tests do not exclude apixaban effect; a drug-calibrated anti-Xa level is needed
quiz.why: Direct factor Xa inhibitors frequently leave PT and aPTT normal at full therapeutic concentrations. A calibrated anti-Xa assay measures the effect. Assuming the anticoagulant has worn off because the routine panel is normal is the dangerous and common error.

quiz.q: Which single result most effectively excludes a clinically relevant dabigatran level?
quiz.why: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor, so the thrombin time is exquisitely sensitive and a normal result essentially excludes a meaningful drug level. The aPTT is prolonged variably and can be normal at lower concentrations, and PT and fibrinogen are not informative.

quiz.q: A bleeding trauma patient's thromboelastography shows a markedly increased LY30 with a normal R time and normal maximum amplitude. What is indicated?
quiz.why: LY30 quantifies how much clot has dissolved at 30 minutes, so a high value means excessive fibrinolysis, which tranexamic acid blocks. A normal R time means factor-driven initiation is intact and a normal maximum amplitude means platelet function is adequate.

quiz.q: A patient with easy bruising, nosebleeds, and heavy menstrual bleeding has a normal platelet count, normal PT, and normal aPTT. What remains on the differential?
choices: Von Willebrand disease or a platelet function defect
quiz.why: Mucocutaneous bleeding with normal counts and normal cascade tests points to a defect in platelet adhesion or function, most commonly von Willebrand disease, which can have a normal aPTT. Hemophilia prolongs the aPTT, warfarin prolongs the PT, and DIC deranges everything.

quiz.q: A urine dipstick reads 3+ blood but microscopy shows no red blood cells. The CK is 31,000 U/L. What explains the dipstick result?
choices: Myoglobin reacting with the heme pad
quiz.why: The blood pad reacts to heme, which is present in myoglobin and free hemoglobin as well as intact red cells. With a CK above 30,000 this is rhabdomyolysis. Menstrual contamination would show abundant red cells, and vitamin C causes false negatives rather than false positives.

quiz.q: A patient with a rising creatinine who takes furosemide has a fractional excretion of sodium of 2.4%. How should this be interpreted?
choices: Uninterpretable on a loop diuretic; use the fractional excretion of urea instead
quiz.why: A loop diuretic forces sodium into the urine, so the fractional excretion of sodium is artificially raised regardless of the underlying cause. Urea handling is less affected, so a fractional excretion of urea under 35% still identifies a pre-renal state.

quiz.q: A euvolemic patient with a sodium of 119 mEq/L has a urine osmolality of 510 mOsm/kg and a urine sodium of 55 mEq/L. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.why: Inappropriately concentrated urine with a high urine sodium in a euvolemic hyponatremic patient means antidiuretic hormone is acting when it should be off. Primary polydipsia and beer potomania produce dilute urine below 100 mOsm/kg, and hypovolemia produces a urine sodium below 20 mEq/L.

quiz.q: A patient with an anion gap acidosis and altered mental status has needle-shaped crystals in the urine sediment. What does this support?
quiz.why: Ethylene glycol is metabolized to oxalic acid, which precipitates with calcium as needle-shaped monohydrate crystals. Methanol produces formic acid and visual loss without crystals, and ketoacidosis and salicylate poisoning do not produce oxalate crystalluria.

quiz.q: A patient suspected of multiple myeloma has a urine dipstick negative for protein. What is the problem?
choices: The dipstick requires a first-morning specimen
The dipstick detects albumin only and misses light chains
quiz.why: The protein pad is albumin-specific, and myeloma spills monoclonal light chains rather than albumin. Suspected myeloma requires urine protein electrophoresis or a sulfosalicylic acid test, both of which detect non-albumin protein.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old has a creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL, flagged by the chart as within normal limits. What does it actually represent?
choices: An error, since children do not produce creatinine
A normal value at any age
Roughly three times this child's baseline, indicating significant kidney injury
quiz.why: A toddler's baseline creatinine is about 0.2 to 0.4 mg/dL because creatinine production depends on muscle mass. A value of 1.0 represents a multi-fold rise and substantial loss of filtration, which the adult reference range conceals completely.

quiz.q: A 7-week-old at a routine visit has a hemoglobin of 9.6 g/dL, is feeding well, and is growing normally. What is the explanation?
quiz.why: Hemoglobin falls to about 9 to 11 g/dL at 6 to 9 weeks as fetal red cells are replaced and erythropoietin is suppressed by improved oxygenation after birth. It is expected in a thriving infant and needs no treatment.

quiz.q: A 3-week-old has a potassium of 6.6 mEq/L on a heel-stick specimen, a normal ECG, and normal feeding. What is the appropriate first action?
quiz.why: Capillary heel-stick samples hemolyze frequently and release intracellular potassium into the specimen. A well infant with a normal ECG and a hemolysis-prone sample needs a repeat draw rather than treatment of a laboratory artifact, which carries its own risks.

quiz.q: A 3-week-old jaundiced infant has a total bilirubin of 9.0 mg/dL with a direct fraction of 3.2 mg/dL. Why is this urgent?
choices: The total is dangerously high for age
A direct bilirubin above 1 mg/dL is never physiologic and raises biliary atresia
quiz.why: Physiologic jaundice is unconjugated. A conjugated fraction above 1 mg/dL or above 20% of the total always means pathology, and biliary atresia must be excluded urgently because surgical outcome depends on operating within the first two months of life.

quiz.q: An 18-day-old has a rectal temperature of 38.4 C, looks well, and has normal vital signs. What is the standard approach?
choices: Blood culture, catheter urine culture, lumbar puncture, and empiric antibiotics
Observation for 4 hours then discharge if well
quiz.why: Under 28 days of age the immune system and the physical examination are both too unreliable to stratify risk, so any fever of 38.0 C or higher earns a complete evaluation and empiric antibiotics. A well appearance does not exclude serious bacterial infection at that age.

quiz.q: The laboratory calls a potassium of 7.2 mEq/L on an anuric dialysis patient who missed two sessions. The monitor shows peaked T waves. What is the correct response?
choices: Treat only after a second value above 7.0
Recollect and wait for the repeat result before treating
Treat immediately and send a confirmatory specimen at the same time
Document the call and reassess with morning labs
quiz.why: The value fits the clinical picture and the ECG confirms it, so delay risks cardiac arrest. Sending a repeat specimen costs nothing and runs in parallel with treatment. Recollecting first is appropriate only when the value is implausible and the patient is well.

quiz.q: Which action completes a critical value callback loop as required?
choices: Leaving a voicemail for the ordering provider
A telephone call to a licensed caregiver with a documented read-back
Sending a secure text message to the care team
Entering the result in the chart with a flag
quiz.why: The loop requires a person who can act to receive the value and repeat it back, with the exchange documented including names and time. A flag, a voicemail, or a one-way message does not confirm that anyone received or understood the result.

quiz.q: A clinician orders a D-dimer on a patient with a Wells score of 6 for pulmonary embolism. What is the flaw?
choices: D-dimer is only valid over age 50
D-dimer must be repeated after 6 hours
D-dimer is insensitive in all patients
At high pretest probability a negative D-dimer cannot exclude the diagnosis, and CT is already indicated
quiz.why: D-dimer is a rule-out test whose usefulness depends on low or intermediate pretest probability. With a Wells score above 4, imaging is indicated regardless of the result, so the test only adds cost, delay, and the chance of false reassurance.

quiz.q: A stable inpatient on the fourth hospital day has unchanged daily CBC and chemistry orders. What is the main argument against continuing them?
choices: Results take too long to be useful
Daily phlebotomy contributes to hospital-acquired anemia and generates false positives that trigger further testing
Laboratory staff cannot process the volume
quiz.why: Routine daily draws can remove 40 to 70 mL per day and are a recognized cause of hospital-acquired anemia, and each additional unindicated test carries about a 5% chance of a false positive that generates a cascade. Choosing Wisely advises against this practice explicitly.

quiz.q: Why is an unlabeled blood bank specimen rejected even when the phlebotomist is certain of the patient identity?
choices: Bedside two-identifier labeling is the only barrier against a fatal ABO-incompatible transfusion
Payers will not reimburse unlabeled specimens
quiz.why: Retrospective certainty is precisely the failure mode that causes wrong-blood-in-tube events, and an ABO-incompatible transfusion can kill within minutes. That is why the rule admits no exceptions regardless of how confident the collector is.

quiz.q: A head CT shows a crescent-shaped hyperdensity along the left convexity that crosses the coronal suture but stops at the midline. What is it?
quiz.why: Subdural blood lies beneath the dura and spreads freely across suture lines but is stopped at the midline by the falx, producing a crescent. Epidural blood is confined by sutures and bulges as a lens, and subarachnoid blood fills sulci and cisterns rather than forming a convexity collection.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old with 2 weeks of progressive confusion after a fall has a CT reported as showing effacement of left-sided sulci and 5 mm of midline shift without obvious hyperdensity. What is the likely finding?
choices: Subacute subdural hematoma that is isodense with brain
quiz.why: Between about one and three weeks, subdural blood becomes isodense with brain and effectively invisible, so it is detected through its mass effect: effaced sulci, a compressed ventricle, and midline shift. The timing after a fall fits exactly.

quiz.q: Why is a head CT for suspected intracranial hemorrhage performed without contrast?
choices: Acute blood is already hyperdense, and contrast would obscure it
Contrast cannot cross the blood-brain barrier
Contrast is nephrotoxic in all head injury patients
quiz.why: Fresh clotted blood measures 50 to 100 Hounsfield units and appears bright white. Iodinated contrast is also bright, so it would mask exactly the finding being sought. Contrast is added when the question is vascular, such as CT angiography for an aneurysm.

quiz.q: A patient with 100 minutes of right hemiparesis has a completely normal non-contrast head CT. What does this support?
choices: This is expected in early ischemia; the scan excludes hemorrhage so thrombolysis can be considered
The study should be repeated with contrast
quiz.why: Ischemic changes generally take 6 to 24 hours to become visible on CT. The purpose of the acute scan is to exclude hemorrhage before thrombolysis, not to demonstrate the infarct. Contrast would obscure blood and is not part of the acute protocol.

quiz.q: A radiology report concludes: 'Findings are nonspecific; clinical correlation recommended.' What is being communicated?
choices: A critical finding requiring immediate callback
The appearance fits several causes and the radiologist needs the clinical picture to narrow it
quiz.why: This standard phrase means the imaging appearance alone does not discriminate between possible causes and the history and examination are required to interpret it. It is neither a statement of normality nor a request for repeat imaging.

quiz.q: Which probe should be selected to obtain a subxiphoid cardiac view between the ribs?
choices: Curvilinear 1-5 MHz with a wide footprint
Phased array 1-5 MHz with a small footprint
quiz.why: Cardiac imaging needs low frequency for depth and a small footprint to fit between ribs, which is the phased array. A linear probe lacks penetration, a curvilinear probe is too wide for intercostal windows, and the endocavitary probe is for transvaginal imaging.

quiz.q: A dyspneic patient has diffuse bilateral vertical comet-tail artifacts extending from the pleural line to the bottom of the screen. What does this indicate?
choices: Interstitial fluid, as in pulmonary edema or ARDS
quiz.why: B-lines are vertical artifacts arising from fluid-thickened interlobular septa, so diffuse bilateral B-lines mean interstitial fluid. Normal lung produces horizontal A-lines, pneumothorax abolishes sliding and B-lines entirely, and an effusion appears as an anechoic collection above the diaphragm.

quiz.q: A patient with acute vertigo and a normal CT has an MRI showing a lesion bright on diffusion weighted imaging and dark on the ADC map. What is this?
quiz.why: Restricted diffusion, bright on DWI with a matching dark ADC, appears within minutes of ischemia and is the earliest imaging sign of acute infarct. Chronic infarcts lose restriction and appear bright on ADC. This is how posterior circulation strokes presenting as vertigo are identified.

quiz.q: A CT abdomen reports dilated proximal small bowel, decompressed distal bowel, and a clearly identified transition point. What does this describe?
quiz.why: A transition point, where dilated bowel abruptly becomes decompressed, is the defining feature of mechanical obstruction. Ileus dilates bowel diffusely with no transition, diverticulitis shows focal colonic wall thickening with fat stranding, and free air indicates perforation.

quiz.q: A patient who works as a metal grinder needs an MRI. What must happen first?
choices: A creatinine to assess gadolinium safety only
Orbital radiographs to exclude an intraocular metal fragment
quiz.why: A retained ferromagnetic fragment in the globe can move in the magnetic field and cause blindness, so anyone with a history of grinding or machining metal gets orbital radiographs before entering the scanner. Renal function matters for gadolinium but does not address this hazard.

quiz.q: A patient vomiting for 4 days has bicarbonate 37 mEq/L, chloride 87 mEq/L, potassium 2.9 mEq/L, and a urine chloride of 7 mEq/L. What does the urine chloride establish?
choices: Saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid loss
Diuretic use within the last 6 hours
quiz.why: A urine chloride below 20 mEq/L means the chloride-depleted kidney is avidly reabsorbing it, which defines the saline-responsive form corrected by sodium chloride and potassium. Mineralocorticoid excess and recent diuretic use both produce a urine chloride above 20 mEq/L.

quiz.q: One hour after a witnessed generalized seizure, a patient's lactate has fallen from 8.4 to 1.7 mmol/L with no specific treatment. What does this indicate?
choices: Occult septic shock that responded to fluid
Post-ictal lactate from anaerobic muscle activity
Laboratory error on the first specimen
quiz.why: Generalized seizures produce a large transient lactate from intense muscle work that clears within about an hour without intervention. Lactate from shock or bowel ischemia does not resolve spontaneously, which makes the rapid clearance the discriminating finding.

quiz.q: A postoperative patient is hypotensive with a hemoglobin falling from 8.1 to 6.2 g/dL, a lactate of 5.0 mmol/L, and free pelvic fluid on bedside ultrasound. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: Septic shock requiring antibiotics and 30 mL/kg of crystalloid
Hemorrhage requiring blood products and surgical control
quiz.why: A falling hemoglobin with free intraperitoneal fluid after surgery is bleeding, and the lactate reflects hypoperfusion from blood loss rather than infection. Crystalloid without blood dilutes clotting factors and worsens the picture; the definitive treatment is surgical.

quiz.q: A patient with the worst headache of their life has a negative CT at 9 hours. Lumbar puncture supernatant is yellow after centrifugation. What does this show?
quiz.why: Xanthochromia is pigment from red cells that have been in the cerebrospinal fluid long enough to break down, which takes 6 to 12 hours. A traumatic tap yields fresh cells that clear from tube one to tube four and leaves a colorless supernatant.

quiz.q: A dyspneic patient has a BNP of 88 pg/mL, a D-dimer of 2,600 ng/mL, a CT filling defect in the right pulmonary artery, a troponin of 62 ng/L, and a dilated right ventricle on echocardiography. What does the troponin represent?
choices: Right ventricular strain from the embolism, marking higher-risk disease
quiz.why: Troponin here reflects right ventricular myocyte strain from acute pressure overload, not a coronary plaque event, and combined with right ventricular dilation it identifies submassive embolism with a worse prognosis. The low BNP had already argued against heart failure as the cause of dyspnea.

scenarios.title: The phone call: a critical potassium at shift change
scenarios.intro: It is `18:45`. The laboratory calls the department with a critical result on a patient in room `9`. You are at the desk with the charge nurse. Room `9` is a `58`-year-old man who came in for a swollen ankle after stepping off a curb. He walked in, he is comfortable, and he has no medical history he can recall. His only medication is a multivitamin.

steps.prompt: The technologist says: 'Critical potassium, room nine, seven point two.' What do you do with that sentence?

choices.text: Read the value back with the patient's name and confirm which specimen and what time it was drawn
choices.feedback: Correct. Read-back with a patient identifier is the whole point of the call, and the draw time and specimen source determine whether the number can even be believed.

choices.text: Say thank you, write it on a sticky note, and pass it on at handover
choices.feedback: The loop is not closed. A note is not a read-back, and a critical value handed across a shift change without documentation is exactly how these are lost.

choices.text: Ask the technologist whether the specimen was hemolyzed and whether the value was repeated
choices.feedback: A good question and one the technologist will already have checked, but the read-back with the identifier comes first so the right patient is attached to the right number.

choices.text: Tell the technologist to call the physician directly and hang up
choices.feedback: Redirecting is reasonable if you are not a licensed caregiver, but hanging up without taking the identifier and value leaves nobody holding the information if the next call fails.

steps.prompt: The technologist confirms the name, says the specimen was drawn at `18:05`, was flagged **moderately hemolyzed**, and the value was repeated on the same tube with the same result. She asks whether you want it recollected.

choices.text: Yes, recollect from a clean peripheral stick without a prolonged tourniquet, and get an ECG on the patient right now
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. Repeating the same tube repeats the same artifact; only a new specimen answers the question. And the ECG is the fastest way to find out whether the potassium is real.

choices.text: No, the repeat on the same tube confirms it; start treatment
choices.feedback: A repeat on the same hemolyzed tube confirms the analyzer, not the patient. Hemolysis releases intracellular potassium into the specimen and is the single most common cause of false hyperkalemia.

choices.text: Recollect, and wait for the new result before doing anything else
choices.feedback: Recollecting is right, but waiting passively wastes `30` minutes. An ECG takes three minutes and tells you whether you can afford to wait at all.

choices.text: Recollect and also check the patient's chart for dialysis, ACE inhibitors, spironolactone, or trimethoprim
choices.feedback: A useful addition. Medication and renal history change the prior probability enormously, and a patient on nothing is far less likely to be genuinely at `7.2`.

steps.prompt: You walk into room `9`. The patient is sitting up on his phone, comfortable, complaining only about his ankle. The ECG is done immediately.

choices.text: A completely normal ECG with normal T waves, a normal PR interval, and a QRS of `88 ms`, which makes a true potassium of `7.2` very unlikely in a well patient
choices.feedback: Correct reasoning. Potassium sets the resting membrane potential, so a genuine `7.2` almost always leaves a trace on the ECG. A clean ECG in a well patient on no relevant drug points hard at the specimen.

choices.text: Treat with calcium gluconate now regardless of the ECG because the number was critical
choices.feedback: Over-treatment. Calcium is given when the potassium is plausible and the ECG or the clinical picture supports it. Here the story, the medications, and the tracing all argue the number is an artifact.

choices.text: The ECG is irrelevant because hyperkalemia does not always change it
choices.feedback: Partly true — the ECG is imperfect and a normal tracing does not guarantee a normal potassium. But combined with a well patient, no relevant medications, and a hemolyzed specimen, it is strong evidence.

choices.text: Normal ECG, and also send a repeat basic metabolic panel with a creatinine to check renal function while waiting
choices.feedback: Sensible. The creatinine on the recollected specimen answers whether there is any renal reason for a genuinely high potassium, and it costs nothing extra.

steps.prompt: The recollected specimen returns at `19:20`: potassium `4.1 mEq/L`, creatinine `0.9 mg/dL`, everything else normal, no hemolysis flag. The oncoming physician asks what happened.

choices.text: Explain that the original tube was hemolyzed, that hemolysis releases intracellular potassium into the specimen, and that the ECG and the recollection both confirmed the true value
choices.feedback: Correct and complete. This is the whole chain in three sentences, and it is what belongs in the note.

choices.text: Say the lab made a mistake
choices.feedback: Unfair and inaccurate. The laboratory measured the specimen correctly and flagged the hemolysis. The error, if there was one, was in the collection.

choices.text: Say the first result was probably wrong and move on without documenting
choices.feedback: The conclusion is right but an undocumented critical value is a compliance failure and leaves the next clinician to rediscover the same confusion.

choices.text: Explain the sequence and add that the draw technique should be reviewed, since a small-gauge needle and a prolonged tourniquet cause most hemolysis
choices.feedback: Correct and constructive. Prolonged tourniquet time, fist clenching, small-bore needles, and drawing through a line are the usual mechanical causes.

steps.prompt: An hour later a second critical call comes: potassium `6.9 mEq/L` on a different patient, a `71`-year-old woman on lisinopril and spironolactone who has been vomiting for three days and has a creatinine of `2.6 mg/dL`. She is drowsy. The ECG shows peaked T waves and a QRS of `126 ms`.

choices.text: Treat immediately — calcium first, then insulin with dextrose and albuterol — and send a confirmatory specimen at the same time
choices.feedback: Correct. This value is entirely plausible: two potassium-retaining drugs, volume depletion, renal impairment, and an ECG that already shows conduction change. Calcium stabilizes the myocardium in minutes; the repeat runs in parallel.

choices.text: Recollect first and wait, as you did with the previous patient
choices.feedback: Harmful. The same protocol applied without thinking. Here the story, the drugs, the creatinine, and the ECG all support the number, and a widening QRS can become an arrest within minutes.

choices.text: Give insulin and dextrose first, holding calcium until the QRS widens further
choices.feedback: The QRS is already `126 ms`. Calcium goes first because it protects the heart within minutes without lowering potassium at all; shifting agents take `15-30` minutes to work.

choices.text: Treat immediately and also stop the lisinopril and spironolactone and arrange nephrology involvement
choices.feedback: Correct and forward-looking. Removing the cause matters as much as the acute treatment, and this combination with volume depletion is a recognized recipe for severe hyperkalemia.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: a critical value is a closed loop and a clinical question at the same time. The loop is read-back with an identifier, documentation, and escalation if nobody answers. The clinical question is whether this number fits this patient, and the answer comes from three things — the story, the medications, and in the case of potassium, the ECG. A repeat run on the same hemolyzed tube confirms the analyzer, not the patient; only a new specimen answers it. Above all, the same value can require opposite responses on the same shift: `7.2` in a well man with a hemolyzed sample and a clean tracing is a recollection, while `6.9` in a vomiting patient on lisinopril and spironolactone with a widening QRS is calcium in the next two minutes. Protocol tells you what steps exist; the patient tells you which one to take.

scenarios.title: Reading the head CT yourself before the report lands
scenarios.intro: An `82`-year-old woman on apixaban for atrial fibrillation had a mechanical fall at home this morning, striking the left side of her head on a doorframe. She did not lose consciousness. Her daughter says she has been 'slower' since lunch. A non-contrast head CT has been done and the images are on the screen; the radiology report is pending. Work through the scan the way a clinician does while waiting.

steps.prompt: Before looking at anything, which question does this scan exist to answer, and why is there no contrast?

choices.text: Is there acute blood; and no contrast because fresh clotted blood is already bright at `50-100` Hounsfield units, so contrast would hide it
choices.feedback: Correct. The whole point of the non-contrast scan is that acute blood is intrinsically hyperdense. Adding iodine, which is also bright, would obscure exactly what you are hunting.

choices.text: Is there an infarct; contrast is omitted to protect the kidneys
choices.feedback: Wrong question and wrong reason. CT is poor at early infarct, and renal concern is not why head CT for trauma is done without contrast.

choices.text: Is there a tumor; contrast would be needed for that
choices.feedback: True that a tumor question needs contrast, but that is not the question in an anticoagulated patient hours after head trauma.

choices.text: Is there blood; and contrast is omitted because it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier
choices.feedback: Right question, wrong physiology. Contrast does cross where the barrier is broken, which is how tumors and abscesses enhance. The reason here is density.

steps.prompt: You start your systematic read. Which order keeps you from being captured by the first thing you notice?

choices.text: Blood, then cisterns, then brain, then bone on bone windows
choices.feedback: Correct. A fixed order means the obvious finding cannot stop the search, and each step asks a different question: is there blood, is there pressure, is the brain symmetric, is the skull intact.

choices.text: Scroll until something looks wrong, then describe it
choices.feedback: This is exactly how second findings get missed. Satisfaction of search is a documented error pattern, and a system is the defense against it.

choices.text: Look only at the side she struck, since that is where the injury is
choices.feedback: A contrecoup injury occurs opposite the impact, and in an anticoagulated patient there may be more than one collection. Both sides get looked at.

choices.text: Blood, cisterns, brain, bone — and also compare with any prior scan in the record
choices.feedback: An excellent addition. A prior study converts a question about whether something is new into an answer, and elderly patients often have one.

steps.prompt: On the left convexity there is a thin crescent-shaped hyperdense collection extending from the frontal region back past the coronal suture. It does not cross the midline. The sulci on the left look less distinct than on the right.

choices.text: Acute subdural hematoma: crescent shaped, crosses suture lines, stopped at the midline by the falx, from torn bridging veins
choices.feedback: Correct on shape, anatomy, and mechanism. Bridging veins are stretched in an atrophic brain, which is why minor trauma in an elderly or alcohol-using patient produces subdurals.

choices.text: Epidural hematoma from a torn middle meningeal artery
choices.feedback: Epidural blood is confined by suture lines and bulges inward as a lens. Crossing the coronal suture rules it out, and epidurals can cross the midline while subdurals cannot.

choices.text: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
choices.feedback: Subarachnoid blood fills the sulci and basal cisterns in a branching star pattern rather than forming a smooth collection along the convexity.

choices.text: Acute subdural, and the indistinct left sulci are mass effect from the collection
choices.feedback: Correct and a step further. Effaced sulci are how you judge whether a thin collection is doing anything, and they are what makes an isodense subacute collection findable at all.

steps.prompt: The basal cisterns are open. The midline measures `3 mm` of shift at the septum pellucidum. Bone windows show no fracture but a small amount of fluid in the left mastoid air cells. Her INR drawn on arrival is `1.1` and the aPTT is `29` seconds, both normal.

choices.text: Normal coagulation studies do not exclude apixaban effect, so proceed with reversal planning and neurosurgical consultation based on the bleed, not the panel
choices.feedback: Correct and the central trap of the case. Direct factor Xa inhibitors frequently leave PT and aPTT entirely normal at full therapeutic levels; a drug-calibrated anti-Xa is the only measuring test.

choices.text: The normal INR and aPTT show the apixaban has worn off, so no reversal is needed
choices.feedback: Dangerously wrong, and a common error. Apixaban is invisible to conventional coagulation tests. The last dose time and the clinical picture guide reversal, not this panel.

choices.text: Send a drug-calibrated anti-Xa level and ask the daughter exactly when the last apixaban dose was taken
choices.feedback: Both are the right moves. The last-dose time is often more available and more actionable than the level, which many laboratories cannot run quickly.

choices.text: Repeat the coagulation panel in two hours to see whether it becomes abnormal
choices.feedback: Waiting for a test that was never going to be abnormal wastes the window in which reversal matters most.

steps.prompt: The final radiology report arrives and reads: 'Thin left convexity subdural hematoma, `6 mm`, with `3 mm` midline shift. No fracture. Fluid in the left mastoid air cells; clinical correlation recommended. Incidental note is made of a `7 mm` right upper lobe pulmonary nodule on the included lung apices; recommend CT chest follow-up in `6-12` months.'

choices.text: Act on the subdural now, and ensure the nodule recommendation is communicated to the patient and her physician so someone owns the follow-up
choices.feedback: Correct. Incidental findings become the treating team's responsibility the moment they are reported, and the commonest failure is that nobody transmits the recommendation at discharge.

choices.text: Ignore the nodule; it is unrelated to the presenting problem
choices.feedback: Unrelated to today, but now documented and known. Incidental findings that are never communicated are a recognized source of delayed cancer diagnoses and of litigation.

choices.text: Order the chest CT tonight
choices.feedback: Over-reaction. The radiologist specified a surveillance interval of `6-12` months precisely because immediate imaging adds radiation and cost without changing anything.

choices.text: Act on the subdural, transmit the nodule recommendation, and note that 'clinical correlation recommended' about the mastoid fluid means the radiologist cannot tell whether it is trauma-related or chronic
choices.feedback: Correct on all three. That phrase signals a nonspecific finding needing your history, and in this context the absence of other basilar skull fracture signs makes chronic fluid more likely.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern to keep: a head CT for trauma is a non-contrast study because fresh blood is already bright, and a fixed reading order — blood, cisterns, brain, bone — protects you from stopping at the first abnormality. Shape and anatomy name the bleed: lens shaped and stopped by sutures is epidural, crescent shaped and stopped by the midline is subdural. Effaced sulci and midline shift are how you judge whether a collection matters, and they are the only way to find a subacute collection that has become isodense with brain. The anticoagulation trap is separate and lethal: a normal INR and aPTT do not exclude apixaban or any other direct oral anticoagulant, so reversal is decided by the bleed and the last dose, never by a reassuring panel. Finally, the report is a document with a vocabulary. Clinical correlation recommended means nonspecific. An incidental finding with a follow-up recommendation is now someone's responsibility, and the discharge is where that responsibility is usually dropped.

scenarios.title: Undifferentiated hypotension: probe in one hand, panel in the other
scenarios.intro: A `66`-year-old man is brought in for weakness and near-syncope at home. He cannot give much history. His wife says he has felt unwell for two days, with some back pain, and that he takes 'a water pill and a blood pressure pill.' He is pale and diaphoretic. You have a bedside ultrasound machine, a monitor, and a laboratory. Nothing has come back yet.

steps.prompt: He is placed on the monitor. The team wants a direction within the first two minutes.

choices.text: Perform a focused ultrasound sequence — heart, inferior vena cava, lungs, abdomen with the aorta, and legs — while blood is drawn and an ECG is obtained
choices.feedback: Correct. In undifferentiated hypotension the probe sorts the four shock categories faster than any laboratory can, and it runs in parallel with the draws rather than instead of them.

choices.text: Give `2 L` of crystalloid and reassess in `20` minutes before any imaging
choices.feedback: Fluid may be right or catastrophically wrong depending on the cause. Volume in cardiogenic shock or a contained aortic rupture is not benign, and twenty minutes is a long time in this patient.

choices.text: Send a full laboratory panel and wait for the lactate and hemoglobin to direct therapy
choices.feedback: The labs matter but they take `30-60` minutes. Bedside ultrasound answers the categorical question in under two.

choices.text: Ultrasound sequence plus an immediate ECG and a point-of-care hemoglobin
choices.feedback: Good addition. The ECG can reveal ischemia or a rhythm as the cause, and a point-of-care hemoglobin returns in minutes rather than the better part of an hour.

steps.prompt: The cardiac views show a vigorously contracting left ventricle, no pericardial effusion, and a right ventricle that is not dilated. The inferior vena cava is small and collapses completely with each breath. Lung fields show sliding bilaterally with A-lines and no B-lines.

choices.text: This excludes tamponade, gross pump failure, large pulmonary embolism, and pneumothorax, and the collapsing vena cava with dry lungs points to hypovolemic or distributive shock
choices.feedback: Correct. Four categories have been narrowed in under two minutes. A-lines with sliding mean neither pulmonary edema nor pneumothorax, which is the other half of the information.

choices.text: A vigorous ventricle means the heart is fine and the cause must be neurologic
choices.feedback: A hyperdynamic ventricle is a finding, not a dismissal: it is what an underfilled or vasodilated heart looks like. Neurogenic shock would not produce a heart rate of `118`.

choices.text: The absence of B-lines means fluid can be given safely without limit
choices.feedback: It does support giving fluid, but 'without limit' is the error. Lungs are rechecked as resuscitation proceeds, and the aorta has not been looked at yet.

choices.text: Correct interpretation, and the aorta and abdomen still need to be imaged before committing to a cause
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Back pain plus hypotension in a `66`-year-old makes the aorta the next view, not an afterthought.

steps.prompt: The abdominal views show an infrarenal aorta measuring `3.1 cm` outer wall to outer wall, no free fluid in Morison's pouch, the splenorenal recess, or the pelvis, and moderate right-sided hydronephrosis. The point-of-care hemoglobin is `11.8 g/dL`.

choices.text: The aorta is mildly dilated but with no free fluid and a normal hemoglobin, rupture is unlikely; the hydronephrosis suggests an obstructed, possibly infected kidney
choices.feedback: Correct synthesis. A `3.1 cm` aorta meets the definition of an aneurysm but a rupture in a hypotensive patient would usually show free fluid and a falling hemoglobin. The hydronephrosis is the new lead.

choices.text: Call vascular surgery for a ruptured aneurysm immediately
choices.feedback: Premature. The size is barely aneurysmal, there is no free fluid, and the hemoglobin is normal. Acting on the first abnormal finding and stopping the search is the error the systematic sequence exists to prevent.

choices.text: Ignore the hydronephrosis; it is a chronic finding in older men
choices.feedback: Possible, but in a hypotensive febrile-range patient with back pain it is the most promising explanation on the screen and must be pursued, not dismissed.

choices.text: Correct synthesis, and send urgent urinalysis, urine culture, blood cultures, and a lactate while starting balanced crystalloid
choices.feedback: The right next moves. An obstructed infected kidney is a drainage emergency, and the cultures must be drawn before antibiotics go in.

steps.prompt: Results return: white count `19,400`, lactate `4.4 mmol/L`, creatinine `2.8 mg/dL` from a baseline of `1.0`, potassium `5.9 mEq/L`, bicarbonate `17 mEq/L`, urinalysis with too-numerous-to-count white cells, positive nitrite, and white cell casts. Temperature is now `38.9 C`.

choices.text: Obstructive pyelonephritis with septic shock and acute kidney injury: cultures, broad antibiotics within the hour, `30 mL/kg` of balanced crystalloid, and urgent urology for decompression
choices.feedback: Correct and complete. The white cell casts prove the infection is in kidney tissue, and an obstructed infected system will not clear with antibiotics alone. Drainage is the definitive treatment.

choices.text: Antibiotics and fluid alone, deferring urology until the morning
choices.feedback: Harmful. A pressurized infected collecting system is a closed abscess that antibiotics cannot sterilize, and it keeps seeding the bloodstream until it is drained.

choices.text: Treat the potassium and the acidosis first and hold antibiotics until cultures result
choices.feedback: Backwards on the antibiotics — every hour of delay in septic shock costs survival. The potassium does need attention, but in parallel, not instead.

choices.text: Correct plan, and also recognize that the potassium of `5.9` and the acidosis are consequences of the kidney injury and will improve with perfusion and drainage
choices.feedback: Accurate. Treating the cause fixes most of the chemistry, though the potassium is still monitored with an ECG in the meantime.

steps.prompt: A stent is placed and he improves. A colleague asks what the ultrasound actually added, given that the urinalysis would have made the diagnosis anyway.

choices.text: It excluded tamponade, pump failure, embolism, pneumothorax, and rupture within two minutes, and it found the obstruction — which the urinalysis alone would never have shown
choices.feedback: Correct. The urinalysis names the infection; only imaging finds the obstruction, and obstruction is what turned a treatable infection into a shock state requiring a procedure.

choices.text: Nothing; the laboratory made the diagnosis and the ultrasound was a formality
choices.feedback: The laboratory took most of an hour and never would have revealed hydronephrosis. Deciding to give fluid safely also depended on seeing a collapsing vena cava and clear lungs.

choices.text: It mainly confirmed that the patient needed fluid
choices.feedback: That was one of several answers it gave, and the least important one. Excluding obstructive and cardiogenic causes changed what could be given safely at all.

choices.text: It gave a direction in two minutes and it also flagged a `3.1 cm` aorta that now needs outpatient surveillance
choices.feedback: Both true. An aneurysm found incidentally still needs a surveillance plan and a communicated recommendation at discharge.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: in undifferentiated hypotension the bedside probe answers the categorical question — is this the pump, the tank, the pipes, or an obstruction — long before any laboratory result exists, and it is done in parallel with the draws rather than instead of them. Run it in a fixed sequence: heart, inferior vena cava, lungs, abdomen with the aorta, legs. A hyperdynamic ventricle with a collapsing vena cava and A-lines means an empty or vasodilated tank and that fluid is safe to give. Stopping at the first abnormal finding, such as a mildly dilated aorta, is the error the sequence exists to prevent; free fluid and a falling hemoglobin are what turn an aneurysm into a rupture. And when the labs arrive they refine rather than replace: white cell casts locate the infection in kidney tissue, but only the image shows the obstruction, and an obstructed infected kidney is drained, not merely treated.
